metadata.title: What's a Cold-Start Interview?
metadata.purpose: Answer what actually gets Claude up to speed on a brand-new matter with no history: a free-form brief written from memory, or a fixed set of questions asked every time. Lands the carry-out that a cold start is fixed by asking the same questions every time, not by writing more.
metadata.source_note: Source sheet's narration carried unfilled '>' template placeholders at every skill-specific fact, and its named source_skill file does not exist on this machine -- see QUESTION.md. This redo reconstructs a generic, defensible cold-start-interview account from the skill's name rather than lifting facts that were never written.
metadata.anchor_pair: B02 -> B03 (jurisdiction -- the detail everyone assumes goes without saying, then answered on request)

beats.narration_text: Someone starts a brand-new legal matter and asks what the brief to Claude should say. Wrong tool. A brief is a data-dump; an interview is a protocol. The real question worth asking: what's the interview?

shot.new_visual_element: Writer types 'New client -- what's the brief?', hesitates on 'brief', corrects to 'interview', lands the real question

beats.note: B00 is Remotion (BrutalistHesitantWriter) per hai-simple SKILL.md WRITER LAW. TIMING LAW: 20-35 word narration + lead_silence_s 0.8 to give the typing a >=9s window; verify media/B00.mp4 >= 8s and that the correction ('brief' -> 'interview') is visible on a late frame.

beats.narration_text: A brand-new matter, and Claude has no memory of your last one — every conversation starts from zero state. The instinct is to just brief it: paste what you think matters and hope that covers it. That works if you value coverage of what you remembered to write. It fails on what you assume goes without saying — jurisdiction, conflicts, retainer scope. The classic gaps aren't the exotic facts. They're the ones so obvious nobody writes them down.

shot.new_visual_element: A 'BRIEF' card with named-detail chips filled in; a dim, unlabeled 'jurisdiction' chip sliding in underneath, unmarked, never joining the card

production_viz.label: A brief only covers what's remembered
production_viz.mechanic: A card labelled 'BRIEF' with three named-detail chips inside it, fully lit ('client name', 'matter type', 'key dates'). A fourth chip slides in from below the card, dim and unlit, passing underneath without touching the brief card. A caption fades in beneath: 'nobody thought to mention it.'

beats.narration_text: A cold-start interview flips the machinery: instead of trusting what you remember to volunteer, Claude runs a fixed script — client, matter type, jurisdiction, conflicts, scope. Same five, every time, in order. They traded your judgment about what's unusual for uniform coverage on every matter. Watch the anchor: jurisdiction. Everyone assumes it goes without saying — which is exactly why a free-form brief leaves it out and a fixed script doesn't.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR -- five fixed question chips lighting in turn, then a dim 'jurisdiction' card set off to the side, marked not volunteered

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR -- five fixed questions, then the skipped one
production_viz.mechanic: Five chips fade in one at a time across the top, each labelled with a fixed question field (client / matter type / jurisdiction / conflicts / scope), then fade out together. THE ANCHOR. A single card appears off to the side, dim and outlined only, reading 'jurisdiction' with a caption 'not volunteered' beneath it -- visibly absent from the five-field set just shown. THIS EXACT CARD RETURNS, ANSWERED, AT B03.

beats.narration_text: Ask directly and jurisdiction gets an answer, even when nobody volunteered it — the fixed question catches what the free brief missed. Honest limit: answering once only covers this matter. The next one starts cold again; Claude doesn't now know your practice. And there's a distinction worth holding — thorough isn't the same as complete. Thorough is a feeling; complete means the same fields get filled every time. Only the fixed script gives you the second one.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR RETURNS -- the dim jurisdiction card lighting up with an answer and sliding into the row of five; then split into 'answered is not remembered' and 'thorough is not complete'

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR RETURNS -- asked, not assumed
production_viz.mechanic: THE B02 DIM CARD RETURNS, identical placement, and fills in with an answer, then slides into a row alongside the other four now-answered fields. It splits into two cards: left reads 'next matter: --' with a struck-through 'REMEMBERED' beneath it, labelled 'answered is not remembered'; right reads 'brief: feels complete' with a faint sixth, unlabeled card appearing at its edge, labelled 'thorough is not complete'.

beats.narration_text: A cold start isn't fixed by writing more — it's fixed by asking the same questions every time. That's the one thing an interview does that a memory can't.

props.quote: A cold start isn't fixed by writing more — it's fixed by asking the same questions every time. That's the one thing an interview does that a memory can't.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini: I'm about to start a brand-new legal matter with you, and you have no memory of my practice. Before I paste any details, run me through a fixed intake — matter type, jurisdiction, any conflicts, retainer scope, and anything else you'd need to open a real file. Ask one at a time, wait for each answer, and don't do anything with the matter until the intake is complete. Go deeper: ask the same model which of its intake questions would still be worth asking on your tenth matter, and which are only worth asking on the first.
